results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No — a creature phasing in does not trigger enter-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing is not a zone change: phasing simply changes a permanent’s phased-in/phased-out status (it’s a static ability that modifies the untap step) and the game treats a permanent that phases in as becoming “phased in,” not as entering the battlefield, so zone-change triggers (including enters-the-battlefield triggers) don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. In particular: phasing is defined as a turn-based action that causes phased-in permanents to phase out and phased-out permanents to phase in during the untap step (702.26a; 703.4a; 502.1); when a permanent phases in its status becomes “phased in” and the game treats it as though it exists (702.26c); but the phasing event doesn’t cause a zone change and zone-change triggers don’t trigger on phasing (702.26d). Enters-the-battlefield and other zone-change triggers are only triggered by objects actually entering the battlefield (603.6a). Note that some phasing-related triggers are exceptions: abilities that trigger when a permanent phases out are checked by “looking back in time” (603.10b), and abilities that trigger when a permanent becomes attached or unattached don’t trigger when that permanent phases in or out (702.26j).

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
Short answer: If an attacking creature has both trample and deathtouch, you only need to assign 1 point of that creature’s combat damage to each blocking creature (minus damage already marked on them and damage being assigned to them at the same time) for assignment to count as “lethal”; any remaining damage can be assigned to the defending player or planeswalker once all blocking creatures have been assigned lethal damage. The rules treat any nonzero damage from a source with deathtouch as lethal for purposes of deciding excess damage to assign with trample.

Why: Trample is a static ability that changes how an attacking creature assigns combat damage: the controller must assign lethal damage to blocking creature(s) first, then any excess can be assigned to the defending player or planeswalker once lethal damage has been assigned to all blockers (or there are no blockers at assignment time) [702.19a, 702.19b]. Deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of combat damage from that source count as lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage; accordingly, when computing how much is “lethal” for trample’s assignment rules, 1 point of damage from a deathtouch source is enough (taking into account damage already marked on the blocker and damage from other creatures being assigned at the same time) [702.2c, 702.19b, 120.4a]. Damage already marked on a creature persists and counts toward lethal calculations until cleanup, so you subtract that marked damage when deciding how much must be assigned now [120.6].

Extra notes and interactions:
- The controller still follows the normal assignment procedure: announce how much of the attacking creature’s damage is assigned to each blocker (up to the lethal amount as modified by deathtouch and existing marked damage) and any remainder to the player or planeswalker [702.19b, 510.1].
- Whether the damage will actually destroy the blocker after damage is dealt (for example because of prevention effects or regeneration) does not change what counts as lethal for assignment — assignment checks ignore abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage actually dealt [702.19b, 120.4a]. If deathtouch damage is dealt and not replaced by regeneration, the creature dealt damage is destroyed by state-based actions [704.5h, 702.2b].
- Multiple instances of deathtouch are redundant and don’t change this interaction [702.2f].

Example (timing assumed: assignment during the combat damage step): A 6/6 attacking creature with trample and deathtouch blocked by a 2/2: its controller may assign 1 damage to the 2/2 (that single point counts as lethal because of deathtouch) and assign the remaining 5 damage to the defending player. If instead there is already 1 damage marked on the 2/2, the attacker could assign 0 additional damage to that blocker and put all 6 damage to the defending player, because the marked damage already reaches lethal for assignment purposes [702.19b, 702.2c, 120.6].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text:
Yes. Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack, and that triggered ability can be countered only by an effect that specifically counters abilities (not by effects that counter only spells).

Definitions and reasoning

- What “storm” is: Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack: “When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.” [702.40a]

- What a triggered ability is: A triggered ability has a trigger condition and an effect and is written like “When/Whenever/At [trigger event], [effect].” [603.1a]

- What happens when storm triggers: When the storm trigger occurs, that triggered ability is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority and becomes the topmost object on the stack. It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, or it otherwise leaves the stack. [603.3]

- Whether it can be countered: Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells, so they can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Because storm is a triggered ability on the stack, it follows this rule. [113.9]

- Note about “can’t be countered” text: If an ability’s text says that ability can’t be countered, that kind of text functions on the stack and overrides the general ability-to-be-countered situation. [113.6g]

If you want to know examples of effects that can or can’t counter a storm trigger, tell me the specific cards or effects and I’ll apply the same rules above.

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: Yes — only if every color that the hybrid symbol represents is within the commander’s color identity. A hybrid mana symbol is considered to be all of its component colors, so a two-color hybrid symbol (for example, {R/G}) makes that card both red and green and therefore it can be included in a Commander deck only if the commander’s color identity contains both of those colors. A monocolored hybrid symbol (for example, {2/R}) includes a colored half and a noncolored half, so it counts only as that color for color-identity purposes and can be included in a deck whose commander has that single color. Definition and rules applied: “hybrid mana symbol” and its components are colored symbols and are all of their component colors ([107.4e]); an object’s colors are the colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost ([202.2d]); the Commander variant uses color identity (the colors of mana symbols in a card’s mana cost or rules text) to determine what cards can be in a deck with a certain commander ([903.4]); and each Commander deck card must have only colors found in the commander’s color identity ([903.5c], with basic-land-type limits explained in [903.5d]).

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No — you can’t respond during the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so spells can’t be cast and activated abilities can’t be activated or resolve during that step [502.4], [117.3a].

Definition of priority: priority is the game state that determines which player may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions; the player with priority may take those actions [117.1].

What happens instead: the untap step is a turn-based step (the first step of the beginning phase) in which certain turn-based actions occur and do not use the stack. All phased-in permanents with phasing the active player controls phase out and phased-out permanents that had phased out under that player’s control phase in simultaneously (phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step) [Untap Step], [703.4a], [702.26a]. Then the active player determines which permanents they control will untap and untaps them all simultaneously; that untap action doesn’t use the stack either [502.3]. The game then checks whether the day/night designation should change as part of the untap step turn-based actions [703.4c], [703.4b], [731.2]. These actions occur without players receiving priority [500.3].

Triggered abilities: any ability that triggers during the untap step is held until the next time a player would receive priority (usually at the beginning of the upkeep); those triggered abilities are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority at the start of the upkeep [502.4], [503.1a], [503.1].

Special case: if an effect causes a player to skip their untap step, the phasing event for that untap simply doesn’t occur that turn [702.26m].

Assumption about timing: this answer assumes the normal sequence of untap-step turn-based actions described above. If you meant some different moment (for example, “right after an untap occurs but before the upkeep begins”), the same rule applies that no player receives priority during the untap step, and priority is next available at the start of the upkeep when those triggered abilities are put on the stack [117.3a], [503.1a].

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text:
Yes. A creature that was attacking remains an attacking creature throughout the end of combat step; they stop being attacking only when they’re removed from combat or when the combat phase ends (which happens as soon as the end of combat step ends, at which point all creatures are removed from combat).

Definition (from the rules): “Attacking Creature. A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal attack during the combat phase (once all costs to attack, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield attacking. It remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.” [Attacking Creature]

Reasoning and important details:
- The Attacking Creature entry states an attacking creature remains so until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends. [Attacking Creature]
- The end of combat step is part of the combat phase; creatures are removed from combat “as soon as the end of combat step ends,” so they remain attacking during the step itself and are removed when that step ends. [511.3]
- A permanent that’s removed from combat (for reasons such as leaving the battlefield, changing controller, phasing out, an effect that specifically removes it from combat, regenerating, or stopping being a creature) stops being an attacking creature at the moment it’s removed. [506.4]
- Abilities that trigger “at end of combat” trigger as the end of combat step begins; effects that last “until end of combat” expire at the end of the combat phase (i.e., when the end of combat step ends). [511.2]
- Exception: if an effect ends the combat phase (for example, Mandate of Peace), follow the special process for ending the combat phase; that process removes all creatures and planeswalkers from combat and skips the end of combat step, and “at end of combat” triggered abilities don’t trigger because the end of combat step is skipped. [724.2d] [724.2e]

So in a normal combat, during the entire end of combat step attacking creatures are still attacking; they cease to be attacking when the end of combat step ends and the game removes creatures from combat (or earlier if they were removed from combat for another reason).

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text:
No — you don’t cast lands. You play a land as a special action (you put the land onto the battlefield), and a land is never a spell.

Definition: To play a land means to put a land onto the battlefield from the zone it’s in (usually your hand). Playing a land is a special action that doesn’t use the stack; it simply happens. (See rules [701.18a], [116.2a], [305.1].)

Key points a player needs to act on:
- Lands aren’t cast as spells and can’t be cast. An object that’s both a land and another card type (for example, an artifact land) can only be played as a land and can’t be cast as a spell. (See rules [305.9], “Artifact Land”.)
- You may play a land only when you have priority, it’s a main phase of your turn, the stack is empty, and you haven’t already played a land this turn (unless a continuous effect changes that). Playing the land does not use the stack and can’t be responded to. (See rules [305.1], [116.2a], [505.6b], [305.2]/[305.2b].)
- Putting a land onto the battlefield because of a spell or ability is not the same as playing a land. Effects that “put” lands onto the battlefield are different and don’t count as having played a land. (See rule [305.4].)
- You can’t play a land on someone else’s turn; ignore any part of an effect that tells you to do so. (See rule [305.3].)
- Note on terminology: “To play a card” can mean to play it as a land or to cast it as a spell, whichever is appropriate; that is why we say you play lands rather than cast them. (See rules [601.1a], [701.18b].)

Assumption/clarification: This answer assumes the usual timing rules and that no specific effect in the game changes the rules quoted above. If an effect specifically replaces or overrides those rules, follow that effect’s text instead.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: Yes. You can sacrifice a creature that was cast for its evoke cost after it has entered the battlefield but before its evoke triggered ability resolves; if the creature is no longer on the battlefield when the evoke triggered ability resolves, that triggered ability can’t make you sacrifice it then. Reasoning and rules: Evoke is an alternate way to cast the card and includes a triggered ability that “When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it” (rule 702.74a). Casting for evoke is an alternative cost paid as part of casting (rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h). The sacrifice required by evoke is the effect of that triggered ability that functions on the battlefield (702.74a), and sacrificial choices occur while a spell or ability is resolving or when another game action allows you to sacrifice (see rule 608.2d’s example showing a player may choose to sacrifice while resolving an effect and that a player who controls no creatures can’t choose that option). If you sacrifice the permanent before the evoke triggered ability resolves, there will be no such permanent to sacrifice when that triggered ability later resolves, so the sacrifice won’t occur then. Note also that one payment of a cost or one sacrifice can’t be retroactively counted as satisfying another spell’s or ability’s cost or effect (rule 118.10).

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes. “Loses all abilities” includes keyword abilities because a keyword is an ability; an effect that removes abilities removes all instances of those abilities. Definition: a “keyword ability” is an ability named by a keyword (for example, flying), i.e. an object “with [keyword ability]” is an object that has that ability. Definition: an effect that removes abilities “loses” or “removes” them; effects that remove an ability remove all instances of it. Supporting points: keyword abilities are abilities, so an ability-removing effect removes them (ability-adding and -removing effects and effects that say an object can’t have an ability are applied in layer 6). Caveat: an effect that defines a characteristic or states a quality of an object (for example by saying a permanent “is [color]” or “can’t be blocked”) is not the same as granting an ability; such characteristic-defining or quality-stating effects aren’t “abilities” granted in the same way and so are treated differently from ability-granting/removing effects.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes. Being at your maximum hand size doesn’t stop you from drawing cards; “maximum hand size” only matters during your cleanup step, when you must discard down. Definition: a player’s maximum hand size is the number of cards they’re allowed to have for the purposes of the cleanup-step discard; a player may have any number of cards in hand at other times and can draw additional cards. Reasoning: Rule [402.2] says a player may have any number of cards in their hand but must discard excess cards as part of their cleanup step. Rule [514.1] (and the turn-based-action phrasing in [703.4n]) explains that discarding down to maximum hand size happens immediately after the cleanup step begins and is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack. Rule [121.2] notes that cards are drawn one at a time, so each draw is an individual action and can increase your hand size before the next cleanup. In short: you can draw while at your maximum hand size; if you end your turn still above your maximum, you will discard down during the cleanup step.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text:
No. A non-creature artifact that is put into a graveyard from the battlefield doesn’t “die.”

Definition and explanation: “Dies” means a creature or planeswalker “dies” if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield (rule 700.4). Because that definition applies only to a creature or a planeswalker, a permanent that is an artifact but not also a creature is not said to “die” when it’s put into its owner’s graveyard from the battlefield (see rules 700.4 and 301.4). If an object is both an artifact and a creature (for example, an artifact creature), it can die because it’s a creature; objects with more than one card type combine those aspects (rule 300.2). Finally, note that noncreature permanents have no power or toughness (rule 208.3), which is part of why the special term “dies” is limited to creatures and planeswalkers.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text:
You lose the game the next time a player would receive priority if you attempt to draw a card when your library is empty. (That loss is a state-based action.)

Definition and primary rule: “Draw” means to put the top card of a player’s library into their hand; draws happen as a turn-based action during the draw step or as the result of an effect that uses the word “draw.” [121.1] [504.1]

Why you lose: If you attempt to draw a card from a library with no cards in it, that player loses the game the next time a player would receive priority; this is handled as a state-based action. [121.4] [704.5b]

Related details you may need:
- If an effect requires you to draw more cards than are left in your library, you draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. [104.3c]
- Replacement effects that replace draws are applied even if no cards could be drawn because your library is empty. [121.6a] [614.11]
- If an effect offers a choice to draw a card and your library is empty, you may choose to do so unless another effect explicitly says that you can’t draw cards. [121.3] [121.3a]
- If an effect moves cards from a library to a zone without using the word “draw,” that isn’t a draw (so it doesn’t cause the draw-from-empty loss). [121.5]
- If an effect attempts to do something impossible (for example, move more cards out of a library than exist), it does as much as possible. [609.3]

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text:

- A mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that could add mana to a player’s mana pool when it resolves and that meets the criteria in rule [605.1] (for example, an activated ability that doesn’t require a target and could add mana). [605.1] [605.1a]

- Triggered mana abilities follow the rules for triggered abilities but also don’t go on the stack in the normal way; they resolve immediately after the event (or ability) that caused them, without waiting for priority, so you can’t respond to them either. [605.4a]

Exception
- If an ability has a target (or otherwise fails to meet the criteria in rule [605.1a]–[605.1b]), it is not a mana ability and instead follows the normal rules for activated or triggered abilities; those non-mana abilities go on the stack and can be responded to. [605.5a]
